en.title: Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival Drops Players Into a Gore-Soaked Labyrinth
en.summary: Saber Interactive's new survival horror game plunges players into a first-person nightmare, wielding puzzle box powers against Pinhead and his Cenobites. Early impressions highlight intense, claustrophobic dread, but is the horror deep enough to truly satisfy?
en.body:
The gates to **Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival** have officially creaked open, and it's a journey into the abyss that's decidedly not for the faint of heart. Released on October 8, 2026, for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S, this first-person survival horror title from Saber Interactive throws players headfirst into a world of visceral terror, where the line between pleasure and pain is as thin and sharp as a newly honed blade.

The game casts players as Aiden, a troubled protagonist on a desperate quest to resurrect his deceased girlfriend. His path leads him to a dark bargain with the enigmatic **Pinhead**, voiced once again by the legendary **Doug Bradley**, requiring him to hunt down members of a death cult and offer their hearts to fuel his grim resurrection. This premise, deeply rooted in the disturbing spirit of the original **Hellraiser** films, sets a grim and compelling stage. However, early impressions suggest that while the game excels at delivering graphic, chain-laden encounters and moments of extreme gore, its narrative delivery can sometimes feel heavy-handed, relying on lengthy exposition dumps that detract from the pacing. The core gameplay loop involves using the powers of the Genesis Configuration puzzle box to navigate terrifying environments and confront the horrors within.

## Into the Labyrinth

**Hellraiser: Revival** leans heavily into its survival horror roots, emphasizing tight spaces and high-anxiety encounters. Comparisons have been drawn to the tense atmosphere of games like **Dead Space** and **Resident Evil 7**, suggesting a commitment to claustrophobic dread. Players will find themselves constantly on edge, fending off gimp-masked cultists and facing the ever-present threat of the Cenobites. The game’s commitment to disturbing imagery is undeniable, with moments that are as likely to make players nervously glance at their surroundings as they are to thrill them with gruesome action. While the visual spectacle of flayed flesh and tightening chains is a significant draw, the overall experience might be hampered by repetitive chase sequences and uninspired boss fights, preventing the game from fully sinking its hooks into players.

## A Fan's Bargain

For fans of **Clive Barker's** iconic franchise, **Hellraiser: Revival** presents a tantalizing, albeit potentially flawed, return to the world of the Cenobites. The inclusion of **Doug Bradley** as **Pinhead** is a massive draw, promising the authentic, unnerving vocal performance that fans have come to expect. The game's faithfulness to the disturbing themes and aesthetic of the first two **Hellraiser** films is a strong point, offering a deep dive into the Labyrinth that many have craved. The 8.0 rating from Screen Rant, which praised its "tight spaces and high anxiety levels," suggests that the game delivers on its promise of terror. However, the potential for narrative pacing issues and repetitive gameplay could be a point of contention for those seeking a more polished or varied horror experience. With no user or critic reviews yet available on Metacritic, the true reception from the wider gaming community remains to be seen.

## What's Next

**Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival** is now available on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S. Players can dive into this new chapter of the horror saga immediately. Further details on potential post-launch content or updates have not yet been announced.

content_raw: From the opening scene of Hellraiser: Revival, in which an intimate moment of sexual fetishism goes horribly wrong for its hero and his lover, this survival horror adventure inspired by Clive Barker’s bloodsoaked ode to BDSM makes it painfully clear that it’s not for the squeamish. So graphic is its ebb and flow between blasting gory holes and bathroom glory holes that the greatest moments of tension I felt playing it were not when I was fending off its hordes of gimp-masked cultists, but rather when I was nervously looking over my shoulder just in case my wife happened to walk in the room. However, peel back the sordid surface layer and Revival doesn’t have much meat to go along with its many buckets of blood. Heavy-handed storytelling, repeated chase sequences, and uninspired boss encounters meant that no matter how many meatsacks had their skin pierced and flayed by chains that tightened onscreen, Hellraiser: Revival never managed to properly get its hooks into me. We play as Aiden, a one liner-spouting everyman with some troubling addiction problems who’s on a quest to bring his newly murdered girlfriend back to life the only way he knows how: by making a pact with pale-skinned series poster boy, Pinhead (voiced with trademark unnerving eloquence by original actor Doug Bradley), to slaughter several members of a local death cult and feed their hearts to her partially reanimated remains. It’s a disturbing premise that’s pretty faithful to the first (and best) two films in the Hellraiser series, but I wish its plot was presented in a more dynamic fashion. The exceedingly gory scenes that featured Pinhead and his cenobite pals always had me glued to the screen, but so much of Revival’s roughly nine-hour story is otherwise delivered in drawn-out exposition dumps spouted by secondary characters, and I never really felt too invested beyond the broad strokes. It’s not a great sign when the chatty in-game merchant is doing most of the heavy lifting here, and I’m not just talking about her ammo crates. Still, at least the shooting is pretty solid, albeit fairly stock standard for the survival horror genre. To be honest, if Revival’s weapon and inventory system borrowed any more from the Resident Evil series you could probably squint and spot a Capcom logo watermarked somewhere onscreen. However, its assortment of upgradeable pistols, shotguns, machine guns, and breakable blades and bats facilitate some fun ways to decapitate and dismember the hedonistic hordes that stand in Aiden’s way, and ammo is scarce enough that I was forced to make use of absolutely everything at my disposal. I admittedly had to toggle off the overzealous aim assist since it would regularly snap to a single enemy when I was trying to target an explosive barrel in the middle of a group, and I also lamented Aiden’s inability to vault over obstacles. This became particularly ludicrous in one instance where I could clearly see a room full of precious items through a wide open window
